input.instructions: Create a compact, accurate blueprint for an 8-to-12-minute educational lesson with exactly ten sequential teaching beats. Do not write full narration. Create exactly three measurable learning objectives. For every beat, provide one distinct complete factual claim, a concrete example, a concise editable visual direction, and one or two exact supplied source IDs. End the claim, example, and visual direction with complete punctuation. Every cited source excerpt must directly support the claim; reuse at least two important technical terms from each cited excerpt so support can be checked locally. Do not invent course assignments, policies, measurements, datasets, instruction encodings, or product behavior that is absent from the supplied excerpts. Keep the claim, example, and visual direction compact; a deterministic local expander will produce the full narration. Sequence the beats from foundations through application and end with a practical analysis checklist. Use only the supplied source excerpts for factual claims. Every factual claim must cite one or more supplied source IDs. Narration must describe information that is essential to understand visuals. Do not imitate a named creator or invent sources.
input.prompt:
Topic: CSCI-453: Computer Architecture. Create a representative course-foundations companion aligned to the official catalog description. It must teach durable concepts and problem-solving methods without claiming to replace the instructor's syllabus. Official catalog description: Computer Architecture is a study of the design of both modern and classic computer hardware. Topics include: a review of classical computer architectures; the design of operation codes and addressing modes, data formats, and their implementation; internal and external bus structures; architectural features to support virtual storage and page-replacement policies, high-level language features, and operating systems. Students will write programs which simulate the organization of several different processor architectures to help further their understanding of design choices. Prerequisites: CSCI-352 or 4003-440 or equivalent courses. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Spring

Source excerpts:

[mit-xv6-book]
The xv6 book explains processes, system calls, traps, page tables, scheduling, locking, file systems, devices, concurrency, and isolation in a small Unix-like kernel. A process combines an address space with execution state and operating-system resources. A system call transfers control from user code to a privileged kernel service. A trap records processor state so the kernel can handle a system call, exception, or interrupt. Page tables map virtual addresses to physical memory with permission bits. The scheduler selects runnable processes and switches processor context. Locks protect invariants when concurrent execution can access shared state. The file system organizes persistent data through inodes, directories, and logged updates. Analysis distinguishes user mode, privileged kernel code, hardware translation, interrupt state, resource ownership, and synchronization invariants.

[riscv-unprivileged]
The RISC-V ISA defines programmer-visible instructions, registers, memory operations, control transfer, exceptions, and ordering behavior. Integer register x0 always reads as zero, while the remaining integer registers hold software-visible values. Load instructions transfer data from memory into registers. Store instructions transfer register data to memory. Branch and jump instructions change control flow. Exceptions report conditions that require a defined transfer of control. Memory-ordering rules constrain how memory operations may be observed. Architecture analysis preserves data dependencies, control dependencies, and architectural state.

[rit-csci-453]
Computer Architecture is a study of the design of both modern and classic computer hardware. Topics include: a review of classical computer architectures; the design of operation codes and addressing modes, data formats, and their implementation; internal and external bus structures; architectural features to support virtual storage and page-replacement policies, high-level language features, and operating systems. Students will write programs which simulate the organization of several different processor architectures to help further their understanding of design choices. Prerequisites: CSCI-352 or 4003-440 or equivalent courses. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Spring

beats.claim: Computer architecture studies the design of both modern and classic computer hardware, focusing on how processors execute instructions and manage data.
beats.example: A modern CPU processes instructions by fetching, decoding, and executing them in a pipeline, while classic architectures like the Von Neumann model separate instruction and data storage.
beats.title: Introduction to Processor Architecture
beats.visualDirection: Display a side-by-side diagram of a classic Von Neumann architecture and a modern pipelined CPU, highlighting the fetch-decode-execute cycle.

beats.claim: Registers are fast, processor-internal memory locations that store software-visible values and control data formats for operations.
beats.example: In RISC-V, integer registers x1 through x31 hold software-visible values, while x0 always reads as zero, ensuring predictable data handling.
beats.title: Registers and Data Formats
beats.visualDirection: Show a register file layout with labeled x0-x31, emphasizing x0's zero-value constraint and data flow into/from memory.

beats.claim: The RISC-V ISA defines programmer-visible instructions, operation codes, and memory operations that dictate how processors execute tasks.
beats.example: Load instructions transfer data from memory into registers, while store instructions transfer register data to memory, forming the core data movement mechanism.
beats.title: Instruction Set and Operation Codes
beats.visualDirection: Illustrate a load/store instruction cycle with arrows showing data flow from memory to register (load) and register to memory (store).

beats.claim: Branch and jump instructions change control flow, allowing processors to execute different code paths based on program logic.
beats.example: Conditional branches redirect execution to different memory addresses when specific register values meet a condition, enabling loops and decision trees.
beats.title: Control Flow and Branching
beats.visualDirection: Draw a control flow graph with a branch instruction splitting into two paths, labeled with condition outcomes.

beats.claim: Addressing modes and data formats determine how processors locate and access memory, impacting performance and design efficiency.
beats.example: Direct addressing loads data from a fixed memory address into a register, while indirect addressing uses a register value as the memory address.
beats.title: Memory Hierarchy and Addressing
beats.visualDirection: Compare direct vs. indirect addressing with memory maps, showing register-to-memory address resolution steps.

beats.claim: Architecture analysis distinguishes user mode, privileged kernel code, and hardware translation to ensure secure system operation.
beats.example: User mode runs unprivileged applications, while privileged kernel code handles system calls and manages hardware resources securely.
beats.title: User Mode vs. Privileged Kernel Mode
beats.visualDirection: Show a two-tier memory model with user space and kernel space, highlighting permission bits and privilege levels.

beats.claim: A system call transfers control from user code to a privileged kernel service, while a trap records processor state for exception handling.
beats.example: When a process requests file I/O, a system call switches to kernel mode, and a trap captures registers to resume execution after completion.
beats.title: System Calls and Traps
beats.visualDirection: Illustrate the system call sequence: user code -> trap -> kernel service -> return to user mode, with state capture points.

beats.claim: Page tables map virtual addresses to physical memory with permission bits, enabling virtual storage and secure isolation.
beats.example: A page table entry translates a virtual address to a physical frame, with read/write/execute bits controlling access permissions.
beats.title: Page Tables and Virtual Memory
beats.visualDirection: Display a page table structure with virtual address bits, frame number, and permission bits, showing translation steps.

beats.claim: The scheduler selects runnable processes and switches processor context, managing concurrency and resource ownership.
beats.example: When a process blocks on I/O, the scheduler picks another runnable process and saves the current processor state for later restoration.
beats.title: Scheduling and Context Switching
beats.visualDirection: Show a process scheduler with a ready queue, blocked queue, and context switch mechanism, highlighting state preservation.

beats.claim: Students simulate processor architectures to understand design choices, applying architectural state, data dependencies, and control dependencies.
beats.example: A simulation tracks register values, memory operations, and control flow to verify that architectural state remains consistent across instructions.
beats.title: Practical Analysis Checklist
beats.visualDirection: Provide a checklist template with fields for architectural state, data dependencies, control dependencies, and simulation output validation.

learningObjectives: Define and explain the core components of a processor architecture, including registers, instruction sets, and memory hierarchy.
Differentiate between user mode and privileged kernel mode, and describe how system calls and traps facilitate secure hardware interaction.
Apply architectural concepts to simulate processor behavior, demonstrating how design choices impact performance and resource management.
